track.name: Engineering Python
track.item_order_rule: Each phase's five lessons are followed by one checkpoint of five questions; the next phase unlocks at full stars.

items.title: Label the circuit
items.intro: Before anyone powers a board, it needs a label: its name and its supply voltage.

recap.title: Circuit labelled
recap.subtitle: Name, voltage and a clean label line, ready for the bench.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What does Python print?
questions.explanation_after_check: name without quotes is the stored text; "name" in quotes is the word itself. Python prints text without its quote marks.
questions.takeaway: So: quotes make text; no quotes means a stored value.
questions.hint_before_check: Look at which name has quote marks around it.

code_note.title: Text and names
code_note.text: Quote marks make text. A name without them refers to a stored value.

science_note.title: Why label a circuit?
science_note.text: Labs share benches and boards. A name and supply voltage on every board stops someone connecting 12 V to a board built for 5 V.

questions.scene_label: A blank label on the board.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Store the supply voltage as a number.
questions.explanation_after_check: 12 is a number, so volts * 2 is 24. In quotes, "12" is text, and text times 2 repeats it: 1212.
questions.takeaway: So: numbers do maths; text in quotes doesn't.
questions.next_bridge: make one label from the name and the voltage.
questions.hint_before_check: Think about what * would do to each option.

code_note.title: Numbers and text
code_note.text: Python stores numbers and text as different types, and each type behaves differently.

science_note.title: Why voltage is a number
science_note.text: Every later calculation, current, power, safe limits, needs the voltage as a number. Stored as text, the maths goes wrong.

questions.ask: What does the label line print?
questions.explanation_after_check: str(volts) turns 12 into "12", and + joins the pieces with their spaces: Circuit A at 12 V.
questions.takeaway: So: + joins text, and str() turns a number into text.
questions.hint_before_check: Look at where the spaces sit.

code_note.title: Joining text
code_note.text: + joins pieces of text into one.

science_note.title: Labels that read like a sentence
science_note.text: "Circuit A at 12 V" can be read at a glance on a crowded bench, which is what safety labels are for.

questions.ask: The technician's script stops. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: volts is a number, and + can't join text to a number, so Python stops. str(volts) turns it into text.
questions.takeaway: So: convert numbers with str() before joining them to text.
questions.next_bridge: write the label for the panel.
questions.hint_before_check: Look for a line that mixes two different types.

code_note.title: Types in one line
code_note.text: Every value has a type, such as text or a number. Some operations need both sides to match.

science_note.title: Why scripts should fail loudly
science_note.text: A script that stops with a clear error is safer than one that prints a wrong label onto a live board.

code_note.title: String prefixes
code_note.text: A letter placed before a quote mark changes how Python reads that text.

science_note.title: Panel labels
science_note.text: Control panels carry short, standard labels so an engineer can check every circuit's supply without opening the case.

items.title: Ohm's law
items.intro: Our 12 V supply drives a 4 Ω resistor. Can you check the current and power before we switch on?

recap.title: Circuit checked
recap.subtitle: The current, the power and a safe rating, all from one script.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What current does Python print?
questions.explanation_after_check: I = V / R = 12 / 4. Python's / always gives a decimal number, a float, so it prints 3.0. // would give 3.
questions.takeaway: So: / always gives a float.
questions.hint_before_check: Think about whether Python keeps decimals when it divides.

code_note.title: Division
code_note.text: Python has more than one division operator, and they give different kinds of number.

science_note.title: Ohm's law
science_note.text: The current through a resistor is the voltage across it divided by its resistance: I = V / R.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 4 Ω

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: / always gives a float in Python; 12 // 4 would give 3.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Work out the power.
questions.explanation_after_check: P = V × I = 12 × 3.0 = 36.0 W. ** would raise 12 to a power instead.
questions.takeaway: So: power is volts times amps.
questions.next_bridge: add a second resistor in series.
questions.hint_before_check: Which operation turns volts and amps into watts?

code_note.title: Arithmetic operators
code_note.text: Python uses symbols such as +, -, *, / and ** for maths.

science_note.title: Electrical power
science_note.text: Power, P = V × I, is how fast a part turns electrical energy into heat or work.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 4 Ω

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: 12 / 3.0 is 4.0, the resistance again.
** is a power in the maths sense: 12 ** 3.0 is 1728.0.
12 + 3.0 is 15.0; power multiplies.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: Add 3 Ω in series. What is the current now?
questions.explanation_after_check: 4 Ω + 3 Ω in series is 7 Ω, so I = 12 / 7 = 1.714..., and round(I, 2) gives 1.71.
questions.takeaway: So: round() sets how many decimals you see.
questions.hint_before_check: Combine the two resistors first.

code_note.title: Rounding
code_note.text: round() controls how many decimal places you see.

science_note.title: Resistors in series
science_note.text: Resistors in a line add up: 4 Ω and 3 Ω behave like one 7 Ω resistor, so the same voltage pushes less current.

questions.scene_label: A second resistor on the board.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 4 Ω + 3 Ω

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: That's before rounding.
That was the current with 4 Ω alone.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Your partner's script says 39 W. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Python works out V ** 2 / 4 first, then adds 3: 36 + 3 = 39.0. It should divide by R_total.
questions.takeaway: So: Python does ** first, then / and *, then + and -.
questions.next_bridge: check the power against the rating.
questions.hint_before_check: Look at which numbers each operation applies to.

code_note.title: Order of operations
code_note.text: Python follows maths order when a line has several operations.

science_note.title: Checking before buying parts
science_note.text: A wrong power figure leads to buying oversized parts, or undersized ones that overheat.

questions.scene_label: A power reading that's too high.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 4 Ω + 3 Ω

states.correct: go state from the right answer

c.feedback: Brackets round V ** 2 change nothing: still 39.0.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Is the power under the 25 W rating?
questions.explanation_after_check: P is 144 / 7, about 20.6 W, so P < 25 is True: the resistor stays within its rating.
questions.takeaway: So: a comparison gives True or False.
questions.hint_before_check: Compare the power with the rating.

code_note.title: Comparisons
code_note.text: Symbols such as < and > compare two values.

science_note.title: Power ratings
science_note.text: Every resistor has a power rating. Running it above that rating overheats it.

picture.description: A scale with coloured bands; the pointer slides to the value on Check.
picture.label: Power against the 25 W rating

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: 20.6 > 25 is False: that asks whether it's over the rating.
== asks whether it's exactly 25: False.
= stores 25 in both names, so Python prints 25.

items.title: Battery life
items.intro: Our robot runs on a 2000 mAh battery and draws 300 mA. How long will it last between charges?

recap.title: Runtime worked out
recap.subtitle: 6 h 40 min, rounded and read safely from typed input.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many hours does the battery last?
questions.explanation_after_check: 2000 / 300 is 6.666... hours. Python prints a float with all its digits.
questions.takeaway: So: Python doesn't round unless you ask.
questions.hint_before_check: Think about what / gives in Python.

code_note.title: Division
code_note.text: Python has more than one division operator.

science_note.title: Battery capacity
science_note.text: mAh means milliamp-hours: a 2000 mAh battery can supply 2000 mA for 1 hour, or less current for longer.

picture.description: A full battery that drains on Check to the charge left; the result pill shows the runtime.
picture.label: A battery draining on Check

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: That would need //, which drops the fraction.
Python doesn't round unless you ask it to.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: How many whole hours?
questions.explanation_after_check: // is floor division: 2000 // 300 is 6 whole hours.
questions.takeaway: So: // keeps whole numbers only.
questions.hint_before_check: You want to drop the part after the decimal point.

code_note.title: Whole-number division
code_note.text: // and % work with whole numbers.

science_note.title: Why whole hours?
science_note.text: Runtimes are quoted as hours and minutes, so a team can plan charging between rounds.

picture.description: A full battery that drains on Check to the charge left; the result pill shows the runtime.
picture.label: The battery draining for whole hours

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: / keeps the fraction: 6.666666666666667.
% gives the remainder, 200.
** raises 2000 to the power 300, an enormous number.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What does the runtime line print?
questions.explanation_after_check: 2000 % 300 is 200 mAh left over; 200 × 60 // 300 is 40 minutes, so it prints 6 h 40 min.
questions.takeaway: So: *, /, // and % share a rank and run left to right.
questions.hint_before_check: Work out the remainder first, then left to right.

code_note.title: Operators of the same rank
code_note.text: *, /, // and % share a rank, so Python works left to right.

science_note.title: Planning charges
science_note.text: Knowing the runtime in hours and minutes tells a team when to swap batteries.

questions.scene_label: The runtime for the pit board.

picture.description: A full battery that drains on Check to the charge left; the result pill shows the runtime.
picture.label: The battery draining to the full runtime

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.label: 6 h 20 min
options.feedback: 20 would come from 200 divided by 10, not from minutes.

options.label: 6.67 h
options.feedback: The f-string fills in whole and mins, not the decimal hours.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The club member types 300, and the script stops. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: input() always gives back text, so 2000 / "300" fails. int() turns the typed text into a number.
questions.takeaway: So: convert typed input before doing maths.
questions.next_bridge: round the runtime for the poster.
questions.hint_before_check: Think about what input() gives back.

code_note.title: Reading input
code_note.text: input() reads what the user types, always as text.

science_note.title: Trusting user input
science_note.text: Values typed by people always arrive as text. Converting them first keeps a calculator from crashing mid-demo.

picture.description: A full battery that drains on Check to the charge left; the result pill shows the runtime.
picture.label: The battery reading once the input is a number

states.correct: go state from the right answer

a.feedback: str() keeps it text: still a TypeError.
Text times 1 is still text: TypeError.

b.feedback: // can't divide by text either: TypeError.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Round the runtime to 1 decimal for the poster.
questions.explanation_after_check: round(hours, 1) keeps one decimal: 6.666... becomes 6.7.
questions.takeaway: So: round(x, n) keeps n decimals.
questions.hint_before_check: round() takes the number and the number of decimals.

code_note.title: Rounding
code_note.text: round() controls how many decimals you see.

science_note.title: Rounding for people
science_note.text: Spec sheets round to a sensible precision. 6.7 hours is honest; 6.666666666666667 suggests precision nobody measured.

picture.description: A full battery that drains on Check to the charge left; the result pill shows the runtime.
picture.label: The battery drain for the poster figure

states.correct: go state from the right answer

items.title: Power budget
items.intro: Before we order a supply, add up what every part draws and check we keep 20% headroom.

recap.title: Budget signed off
recap.subtitle: 6.75 W needed, 0.5625 A drawn, and 32.5% headroom.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What total power does Python print?
questions.explanation_after_check: 0.5 + 6.0 + 0.25 = 6.75 watts in total.
questions.takeaway: So: floats add like decimals.
questions.next_bridge: find the current the supply must give.
questions.hint_before_check: Add the three parts.

code_note.title: Adding floats
code_note.text: Numbers with a decimal point are floats in Python.

science_note.title: A power budget
science_note.text: Engineers list what every part draws before choosing a supply, so the supply is never the weakest link.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: Power drawn by each part, in W

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: Python doesn't round unless you ask.
These are decimals, not whole numbers.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: What current does a 12 V supply give?
questions.takeaway: So: rearrange P = V × I to I = P / V.
questions.hint_before_check: Power is volts times amps.

code_note.title: Rearranging a formula
code_note.text: Code can rearrange a formula the same way you would on paper.

science_note.title: Current from power
science_note.text: Supplies are rated in amps as well as volts. The current tells you which supply, wires and fuse to choose.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 21.33 Ω

// rounds down to 0.0 here.
% gives the remainder, 6.75.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: Two sensors draw 0.1 W and 0.2 W. What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the sum is a tiny bit off: 0.30000000000000004. Round before you compare or display.
questions.takeaway: So: floats are close approximations.
questions.hint_before_check: Some decimals can't be stored exactly in binary.

code_note.title: Floats are approximate
code_note.text: Computers store most decimals as close approximations.

science_note.title: Why engineers round
science_note.text: Tiny float errors don't matter in a power budget, but 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. Round, or compare with a tolerance.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: Two sensors, in W

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: That's the maths answer, but Python stores floats in binary.
Python doesn't pad decimals like that.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Headroom shows 9.325, not 0.325. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Python divides first: 10 − 0.675 = 9.325. Brackets make it (supply − need) / supply = 0.325.
questions.takeaway: So: brackets decide what a division covers.
questions.next_bridge: check the headroom is at least 20%.
questions.hint_before_check: Look at which numbers the division applies to.

code_note.title: Order of operations
code_note.text: Python follows maths order when a line has several operations.

science_note.title: Headroom
science_note.text: Headroom is the spare share of the supply. Parts draw more when they start up or warm, so engineers keep a margin.

questions.scene_label: A headroom figure that can't be right.

picture.description: A scale with coloured bands; the pointer slides to the value on Check.

questions.explanation_after_check: 0.325 >= 0.2 is True: the supply keeps 32.5% headroom.
questions.takeaway: So: >= includes the limit itself.
questions.hint_before_check: 20% as a fraction of 1.

code_note.title: Comparisons
code_note.text: >= compares two values and gives True or False.

science_note.title: Signing off a design
science_note.text: A design review asks for evidence. A True next to "20% headroom" is a check anyone can rerun.

picture.description: A scale with coloured bands; the pointer slides to the value on Check.
picture.label: Headroom from 0 to 60 percent

items.title: Fuse rating
items.intro: A 60 W heater runs on a 12 V supply. Pick a fuse that carries its current with 25% to spare.

recap.title: Fuse chosen
recap.subtitle: Current from power, a 25% margin, and rounding up, not down.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What current does the heater draw?
questions.explanation_after_check: I = P / V = 60 / 12 = 5.0 A. / gives a float.
questions.takeaway: So: I = P / V.
questions.hint_before_check: I = P / V.

code_note.title: Reusing formulas
code_note.text: The same P = V × I gives current when you divide.

science_note.title: Fuses
science_note.text: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when too much current flows, cutting the circuit before the wiring overheats.

picture.description: A supply and resistors in a loop; current dots flow round the wire, faster for more amps; the result pill shows the reading.
picture.label: Circuit: a 12 V supply and 2.4 Ω

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: / always gives a float: 5.0.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Add 25% to the current.
questions.explanation_after_check: 5.0 × 1.25 = 6.25 A: the current plus a quarter.
questions.takeaway: So: a percentage margin is a multiplier.
questions.hint_before_check: 125% of a value is the value times 1.25.

code_note.title: Multipliers
code_note.text: Adding 25% is the same as multiplying by 1.25.

science_note.title: Fuse margins
science_note.text: A fuse rated exactly at the load current can blow from small surges, so fuses are chosen with a margin above it.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: Current in A

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: That takes some away: 4.0.
That takes 1.25 away: 3.75.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: Fuses come in whole amps. What does round() give?
questions.explanation_after_check: round() goes to the nearest whole number, and 6.25 is nearer 6. A 6 A fuse is below 6.25 A, so it would blow.
questions.takeaway: So: round() can round down.
questions.hint_before_check: round() goes to the nearest whole number.

code_note.title: round()
code_note.text: round() with no decimals gives the nearest whole number.

science_note.title: Sizing up
science_note.text: A fuse must be at or above the margin, never below it.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: Current in A

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: 6.25 is nearer 6 than 7.
With no second number, round() gives a whole number.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What does int() give for 6.75?
questions.explanation_after_check: int() cuts the decimals off, so 6.75 becomes 6. It never rounds up.
questions.takeaway: So: int() always goes down for positive numbers.
questions.hint_before_check: int() doesn't round; it cuts.

code_note.title: int()
code_note.text: int() keeps the whole-number part and drops the rest.

science_note.title: Rounding rules
science_note.text: Rounding a fuse down is the unsafe direction; a fuse rule always rounds up.

picture.description: Bars grow one after another against an optional reference line; value labels and a result note.
picture.label: Current in A

states.correct: go state from the right answer

options.feedback: int() doesn't round to the nearest number; it cuts.

questions.ask: A 6 A fuse would blow at 6.25 A. Fix the size.
questions.explanation_after_check: round(6.25) is 6, below the 6.25 A needed. math.ceil() always rounds up: 7.
questions.takeaway: So: math.ceil() rounds up.
questions.hint_before_check: You need the next whole number up.

code_note.title: math.ceil()
code_note.text: The math module's ceil() gives the next whole number up.

science_note.title: Standard fuses
science_note.text: Choose the next fuse size above the margin, so normal running never blows it.

items.title: Part numbers
items.intro: Every resistor drawer has a code like R470K: a type letter, then the value. Read the codes before you pick parts.

recap.title: Codes read
